description:
TADAAAAA! Hello, we are Teddy, Ann, Dylan, Alan. 

We are four Taiwanese freshman students @ Purdue in majors related to technology. Eager to bring our skills together and solve real-world issues hands-on, we formed a team and joined this challenge. 

We joined this on our own and isn't affiliated with Purdue University.
summary: TADAmoon is a visualization tool that aims to support agile mission planning while bringing lunar exploration closer to the public. We have developed an intuitive, highly visual web app that prioritizes swift scenario comparison for different lunar landing sites based on their power generation potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows. Existing tools often feature overly complex interfaces that slow down decision-making and fragment critical data across multiple platforms. To solve this, we developed a unified, intuitive dashboard using NASA data that prioritizes efficiency and rapid comparison without compromising technical accuracy. Our design bridges the gap between technical precision and public accessibility, making lunar exploration more approachable without losing the depth needed for substantial mission planning.
details:
Core Features & Interface

TADAmoon is designed to streamline mission planning for lunar landing on different sites at the moon’s south pole. Our web app adopts a clean and engaging UI to allow users to compare various potential landing sites and dates, including time, efficiently. At the focal point of the website stands the high-resolution polar projection map of the south pole, which is mapped from real data from NASA’s moon texture data. It is interactive and by clicking on different dots representing existing candidate landing sites, users can select which landing site’s data they want to view.

Figure 1: screenshot of Polar Projection Map from our website (TADAmoon)

Not only does the home page of TADAmoon visualize the landing sites on a polar projection map, it also includes a 3D model of the terrain profile of the surface. By sliding the timeline below the 3D model, users can watch the Sun and Earth interact with an accurate 3D lunar horizon to immediately see how terrain shadows affect power and communication over time. Rather than relying on generic 3D assets, every terrain shadow and celestial orbit in our interface is driven strictly by real lunar topography and orbital mechanics data. 

Figure 2: screenshot of 3D Terrain Profile from our website (TADAmoon)

Orbit simulator:

Using the orbit simulator, the user inputs a specific date and time to start the simulation. The simulator illustrates how the Sun, Earth, and Moon orbit. This was the initial idea for creating our entire website, marking a remarkable milestone for our group. This is also the most understandable monitor of the whole website for the moon's orbit.

Figure 3: screenshot of Orbit Simulator from our website (TADAmoon)

Creative Approach to Data

While we were looking at existing tools for reference, as students that are not in aerospace-related majors, we found it challenging to navigate and understand how the raw data presented contributes to mission planning. For example, ephemeris tables and topographic CSVs were deemed by us as unreadable. At that moment, our creative vision formed — we decided to make the data instantly visible in many different forms all in a web page. 

Instead of giving users a raw spreadsheet of sunrise and sunset times, our team graphed the Sun and Earth’s elevation paths directly against the local skyline over a full month, then highlighting the 14-day window in faint yellow. This creative approach allows mission planners to intuitively see exactly when and for how long a signal will drop or a shadow will fall just by looking at where the lines cross the zero-axis. It also supports CSV export. 


Figure 4: screenshot of 30-Day Skyline Clearance from our website (TADAmoon)

We also translated raw ephemeris data into simple numbers that are easy to compare intuitively on a cross table. This will be further discussed in the next section. Moreover, our interface also provides intuitive progress bars (e.g., 67% Sunlight Duration) and plain-text warnings (e.g., "The longest shadow exceeds the modeled battery endurance"). This plainly tells the user why the data matters and how it affects the mission’s planning. 

Figure 5: screenshot of Site Assessment from our website (TADAmoon)

Impact & Benefits

Our tool bridges the gap between raw aerospace data, mission planning, and public awareness. For mission planning, our tool accelerates the evaluation process of landing dates and locations by allowing mission planners to rapidly assess alternative sites, power potential, and communication windows to the Earth by looking at our quick comparison tool. This is especially helpful when hardware challenges occur and mission constraints and timeline shifts, usually unexpectedly. 

A notable point is that our comparison tool doesn't just put two data tables next to each other. It creatively synchronizes two different 3D terrain profiles and skyline graphs on the same screen, allowing users to visually weigh the trade-offs between two locations in a single glance.

Figure 6: screenshot of Comparison Tool from our website (TADAmoon)

Furthermore, our platform is purposefully designed to accommodate users across all skill levels. By visualizing the complex data in the mission in an engaging and interactive format, TADAmoon helps educators, students, and anyone who’s interested in lunar exploration gain a fundamental understanding of the challenges involved in lunar missions, and provide them the option to delve deeper into the data if they wish to. 

Last but not least, choosing to design and build TADAmoon as a web app allows users to access it on different devices, which enables significant flexibility, whether it’s for mission planners, educators, or the public.

Design and Technical Considerations

We processed the 5-meter-per-pixel NASA LOLA elevation models using Python via libraries like rasterio and numpy to construct a mathematically accurate 3D polar terrain model. We especially took into consideration that the Moon has no atmosphere, which meant that calculating the horizon required building the actual physical slopes and craters of the south pole surface, without needing to account for atmospheric refraction. 

To track solar power and the direct-to-Earth communication windows in real time, our system imported NASA JPL’s de421.bsp ephemeris and MOON_ME_DE421 libration kernels with Skyfield to compute the topocentric altitude and azimuth of the Sun and Earth from the lander’s coordinates, then uses our 360° skyline map at those exact points to see if they are visible or blocked by a mountain. This allows our tool to account for Earth's libration (wobble) and orbital variations. For solar power, the engine models the Sun’s ~0.266° angular disk radius to distinguish between full illumination, partial ridge eclipses, and complete shadow. Finally, by scanning a 30-day forecast grid and subdividing every horizon crossing into 1-minute ephemeris steps, the application delivers real-time countdowns to the next Sunset, Sunrise, Earthset, or Earthrise alongside cumulative sunlight percentages, peak/mean solar elevation angles, and maximum continuous shadow durations.

As we all worked on different components individually and locally on our devices using different languages and virtual environments, we struggled to combine our finished products. Hence, after all of these steps, we compiled everything onto Google AI Studio to combine them smoothly and improve the aesthetics of the UI. We acknowledge that the finished product is put together via AI, but the individual components and the logic and code behind them, and most importantly – the ideation and brainstorming behind all this – are all handled by our hardworking team members.
dataRefs: NASA High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites
